newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-NEW LABOUR, SAME OLD WEATHER FOR AUSTRALIAN TOURISTS.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-NEW LABOUR, SAME OLD WEATHER FOR AUSTRALIAN TOURISTS.

text.p: New Labour, same old weather.
For the first time since Greg Chappell's side 20 years ago, the Australian cricketers arrived this month to an England headed by a Labour government.
But while the political map has changed radically, the weather remains depressingly familiar.
The Australians have spent much of the first week dodging showers in temperatures which struggled to reach double figures.
On Tuesday their already abbreviated programme was further shortened when the one-day match against Durham was abandoned.
Despite their lack of match practice, the Australians are enviably relaxed before the first of three one-day internationals starting at Headingley on Thursday.
And none more so than captain Mark Taylor, who scored 76 runs in a one-day match against Northamptonshire without looking in particularly good touch.
Taylor has played an impeccably straight bat to a barrage of deliveries from the media after conceding before leaving Sydney that he needed to make runs to keep his test place.
"I can do it," he said this week. "If I don't do it then I will have to drop myself."
Australia, by common consensus, are the top team in the world and have held the Ashes since 1989, Taylor's first trip to England.
But no hint of complacency will interfere with their preparation for the one-day series and the six tests afterwards.
Taylor has been quick to reject suggestions that his team need only take the field to win the series.
"Definitely not," he replied. "This is something we have got to guard against. We had it here in 1989 when people said England just had to turn up to win."
Shane Warne, whose wrist spin destroyed England in 1993 and again in Australia in 1994-95. added: "I actually think it's going to be a bit closer than what people think.
"Darren Gough's back in the England side and performing well. He's going to add a bit of spark and a bit of heart to the side."
England's 15-man squad for the three one-dayers is a somewhat cautious mix of the new and the old.
Nineteen-year-old all-rounder Ben Hollioake, yet to be capped for Surrey, joins his older brother Adam in a rare gamble on youth.
But 31-year-old seamer Phil DeFreitas, who will never now fulfill his potential at test level, is also included.
John Crawley, not previously regarded as a one-day player but considered the best player of spin bowling in England, has been picked to help offset the obvious threat of Warne.
In the Australian side, Taylor will probably be partnered at opener by Mark Waugh with the recalled Michael Slater slotting in down the order.

Green, seaming pitches, the norm in an English May should theoretically help the home side. Against this Australia have a talented array of batsmen and strike bowler Glenn McGrath, who has all the attributes to become a huge success in English conditions.
